A fortuity is something that happens purely by chance — not because anyone planned it, caused it, or intended it. It is an event, circumstance, or result that comes about through random luck rather than through design, effort, or reason.

Think of it this way: if you drop a coin and it lands perfectly standing upright on its edge, that is a fortuity. Nobody made it happen. Nobody could have reliably made it happen. It just did — by the sheer randomness of the universe.
Two Ways the Word Is Used

The word "fortuity" works in two related but slightly different ways:

1. As a "thing" — a specific chance event
Here, a fortuity is a concrete, individual happening that occurred by accident or luck. You can use it with the article "a" or "an," and you can make it plural: fortuities.

"Their friendship began as a fortuity — they had simply sat next to each other on the wrong train."

"Life is full of fortuities that quietly redirect our paths."

2. As a quality or condition — the state of being accidental
Here, fortuity refers to the abstract quality of randomness or chanciness itself — the sheer fact that something was not controlled or intended.

"The fortuity of his discovery made it no less remarkable." (Meaning: the fact that it was accidental didn't make it less remarkable.)

"There is a certain fortuity to how most great ideas emerge." (Meaning: a quality of randomness, of "it just happened that way.")
A Crucial Point: It Is Completely Neutral

This is one of the most important things to understand about fortuity. It does not mean good luck, and it does not mean bad luck. It simply means unplanned chance — the outcome could be wonderful, terrible, or entirely ordinary.

  • Stumbling upon a wallet full of cash on the street → a fortuity.
  • Stumbling and twisting your ankle on a crack in the road → also a fortuity.
  • Two strangers who happen to be on the same flight and fall in love → a fortuity.

The word describes how something happened (by chance, not by design), not what it resulted in.
How It Differs From Words That Feel Similar

Understanding a word gets much sharper when you see how it sits beside its neighbors.

Fortuity vs. Luck / Fortune
"Luck" and "fortune" almost always carry a positive flavor — we say "good luck," "he was fortunate." Fortuity carries no such flavor. It is colder and more precise: it just means "chance was the cause," full stop.

Fortuity vs. Coincidence
A coincidence is specifically when two or more separate things happen at the same time or place in a surprising way — the emphasis is on the overlap between events. A fortuity is broader: any single event that happens by chance qualifies, even if nothing else "coincides" with it.

Fortuity vs. Accident
In everyday speech, "accident" often implies something went wrong — a car accident, an accident at work. Fortuity has no such negative pull. Also, "accident" is a very casual, everyday word; fortuity is more formal and precise in tone.

Fortuity vs. Chance
"Chance" is the closest everyday synonym. But "chance" is a very general, informal word with many uses ("take a chance," "by chance," "what are the chances?"). Fortuity is a more specific and formal term that is used strictly to describe an unplanned event or the quality of being unplanned — it gives your sentence a more precise, elevated tone.
Why Writers and Thinkers Use This Word

"Fortuity" earns its place in the language because it captures something that no other common English word captures as cleanly: the idea that something happened outside of any controlling intention, without the baggage of implying good luck, bad luck, or a collision of events. When someone wants to say, with precision and elegance, "this was not designed — chance made this happen," fortuity is the exact word for it.

It often appears in philosophical writing, literary prose, legal language, and careful journalism — anywhere precision about the nature of causation matters.
Locking It In: A Few Final Examples

ContextSentence
Science"The invention of the microwave oven was a fortuity — an engineer noticed radar waves had melted his candy bar."
Relationships"Their reunion after twenty years was a fortuity neither could have scripted."
Philosophy"He refused to accept that his success was mere fortuity; he believed in his own effort."
Everyday life"The fortuity of finding her keys in the last pocket she checked saved her an hour of searching."

To lock it in with examples: The invention of the microwave oven is often cited as a fortuity — an engineer simply noticed that radar waves had melted a candy bar in his pocket. The reunion of two long-lost friends at an airport is a fortuity. A philosopher might argue that believing in fortuity undermines the idea of personal agency. And in the smallest moments of life — finding your keys in the very last pocket you check — there are tiny fortuities too.

A fortuity is any event, circumstance, or result that happened by chance rather than by plan or intention — and the word carries no built-in judgment about whether that chance outcome was good or bad.
